lessons.title: Lesson 1: Coordinates and their history

activities.prompt: How did ancient people give exact places a number?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Coordinates Through Time
activities.body: A coordinate system is a structured framework for describing locations. It uses numbers to show exact physical positions. Systematic grids began thousands of years ago. Ancient streets ran North–South and East–West, about 10 metres apart. Merchants counted units to find shops. Baudhāyana later used these lines. Ptolemy built on earlier work. Āryabhaṭa replaced Greek chords with sines. A longitude meridian is a line for measuring other places.
keyPoints: Coordinates use numbers for exact physical locations.
Merchants used ancient street grids to count their way to shops.
Ujjayinī was central for measuring places, while Brahmagupta formalised zero in algebra.
activities.explanation: You can now connect coordinates with grids, history, and measurement.

5 + 3 = 8 grid units.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: The two-dimensional Cartesian system

activities.prompt: How can we describe exactly where something is?

activities.title: Using two axes
activities.body: A coordinate system uses two lines at right angles. The x-axis is horizontal. The y-axis is vertical. They meet at the origin O, which has coordinates (0, 0). Equal distance units are marked on both lines. You can use these axes to locate any point in two-dimensional space. Rightwards and upwards are positive. Leftwards and downwards are negative. The number line studied earlier is one-dimensional.
keyPoints: The x-axis is horizontal and the y-axis is vertical.
The axes meet at the origin O.
Positive and negative directions help locate points.
activities.explanation: The two axes work together to show a point's position.

Rightward distances from O are positive, so the x-coordinate is 3.
The x-coordinate is 3 units.

activities.title: Points, axes and quadrants

activities.title: Distance between two points
activities.body: The distance between two points is the length of the segment joining them. When the points lie on the axes, you can find this distance. The same works when the joining segment is parallel to an axis. For any two points in the xy-plane, the Baudhāyana–Pythagoras Theorem works. It combines the squares of the horizontal and vertical changes.

Axis changes help find distance

activities.prompt: How does a coordinate system differ from the ancient city’s grid-based street arrangement?
activities.answer: A coordinate system is a structured framework for describing locations by using numbers. The ancient city grid was a systematic use of that general idea: streets were arranged precisely North–South and East–West, about 10 metres apart, so a merchant could count units in both directions to find a shop. Baudhāyana later used East–West and North–South lines, and Ujjayinī served as the central longitude meridian. The grid was therefore a practical, organised way to describe positions through numbers.

Explains its use of numbers to describe locations
Describes the ancient North–South and East–West grid
Explains how counting units helped locate a shop

Each new stage adds 2 squares. Therefore, the difference between neighbouring stage counts stays the same. This constant difference shows that stage number and square count have a linear relationship.

Each new stage adds 2 squares.
A degree-one polynomial is linear.

activities.prompt: Explain how a one-variable polynomial differs from a linear polynomial.
activities.answer: One-variable and univariate are two names for the same kind of expression: one that involves one variable and its powers. A linear polynomial is identified by its degree, not merely by having one variable. A polynomial of degree 1 is called linear. Therefore, an expression may be univariate without being linear. The information that an expression has one variable alone does not establish its degree. To call it linear, its degree must be shown to be 1.

A linear polynomial has degree 1.

activities.prompt: How did people learn to count before written numbers existed?

activities.title: Why People Started Counting
activities.body: Counting was an early need. They matched objects one-to-one. This means each object had one matching object. A herder used this with cows. He placed a pebble for each cow leaving the settlement. He removed one pebble for each cow returning in the evening. Natural numbers are counting numbers for this need. Numbers were recorded as tally marks carved into bone. Lebombo and Ishango bones show counting records.
keyPoints: Counting began as a practical need.
Pebbles helped herders match cows.
Tally marks on bone recorded numbers.
activities.explanation: Counting grew from practical needs, and people carved marks to record it.

activities.title: How trade led towards zero
activities.body: Large numbers became necessary as civilisations advanced. Standardised weights and measures helped trade. Lothal and Harappa were town centres. India used place values and powers of 10. Place values show a digit's place. This helped lead to zero. The Ṛigveda used quantities in powers of 10. Babylonians and Mayans used placeholders for empty columns. Brahmagupta transformed the void, or emptiness, into a number. Śhūnyatā was a goal of yoga and meditation.
keyPoints: Lothal and Harappa were important urban centres
Trade needed standardised weights and measures
India's number system used place values and powers of 10

Positive natural numbers, their negative counterparts and zero form the integers.

Adding or subtracting zero changes nothing.
Fortunes were positive, while debts were negative.

gen.template: A rational decimal repeats the block 142857 {n} times. The block is first multiplied by 2, and the resulting block is then repeated {n} times. How many digits are in the resulting repeated part?
steps: Multiply {given_block} by {multiplier}.
The new block is {twice_block}, and it has {block_digits} digits.
Repeat the new block {n} times.
{total_digits} = {answer} digits.
gen.hint: First multiply 142857 by two to find the new block.

activities.explanation: Watch how it is solved.

activities.prompt: In a contradiction test for irrationality, suppose a fraction has numerator 2 x 5 and denominator 2 x 5. After dividing both even numbers by 2, what is the sum of the new numerator and new denominator?
activities.explanation: A proof by contradiction assumes that the number being tested is rational. The numerator 10 and denominator 10 are both even, so divide each by 2. The reduced numerator is 5 and the reduced denominator is 5. 10 = 10.
steps: A proof by contradiction assumes that the number being tested is rational.
The numerator 10 and denominator 10 are both even, so divide each by 2.
The reduced numerator is 5 and the reduced denominator is 5.
activities.hint: In the contradiction step, divide both even parts by two.

steps: A proof by contradiction assumes that the number being tested is rational.
The numerator {numerator} and denominator {denominator} are both even, so divide each by {divisor}.
The reduced numerator is {reduced_numerator} and the reduced denominator is {reduced_denominator}.

activities.prompt: A decimal never ends or repeats. What kind of number is it?
options: It is irrational, because this decimal never ends or repeats.
It is rational, because long division has not stopped yet.
It is rational, because the remainder is always nonzero.
It cannot be placed on the real number line at all.

why.It is rational, because long division ha: This confuses continuing division with a repeating rational decimal.
why.It is rational, because the remainder is: This wrongly assumes that any nonzero remainder makes a number rational.
why.It cannot be placed on the real number l: This wrongly thinks irrational numbers are outside the real number line.

activities.explanation: This is right because irrational decimals never end or repeat.

activities.prompt: To prove √2 is irrational, what should a student assume first?
options: It is rational, because contradiction starts from the opposite.
It is irrational, because that is the wanted conclusion.
It is even, because both parts must become even.
It terminates, because every rational decimal must end.

why.It is irrational, because that is the wa: This puts the wanted conclusion at the start instead of assuming its opposite.
why.It is even, because both parts must beco: This moves the proof's final result to its starting assumption.

activities.explanation: This is right because proof by contradiction assumes the opposite claim.

activities.prompt: An irrationality proof ends with an even numerator and denominator. What happens?
options: It has reached a contradiction in the assumed rationality.
It has found the simplest form, since both parts are even.
It has shown that the decimal must repeat forever.
It has shown that the number leaves the real line.

why.It has found the simplest form, since bo: This mistakes the proof's final even parts for a normal finish.
why.It has shown that the decimal must repea: This wrongly links the even parts to a repeating decimal.
why.It has shown that the number leaves the: This wrongly treats an irrational number as outside the real line.

activities.explanation: This is right because the even numerator and denominator complete the contradiction.

activities.prompt: Pi is a circumference-to-diameter ratio. Mādhava used an infinite sum. What follows?
options: It is irrational, and it lies on the real number line.
It is rational, because a ratio must be rational.
It is imaginary, because an infinite sum needs the letter i.
It is outside the real line, because pi never ends.

why.It is rational, because a ratio must be: This confuses being a ratio with being rational.
why.It is imaginary, because an infinite sum: This confuses an irrational number with an invented imaginary number.
why.It is outside the real line, because pi: This wrongly thinks irrational numbers are outside the real line.

activities.explanation: This is right because pi is irrational and irrational numbers are real.

activities.context: Early people counted because it was a practical need, matching each object with one item. A herder placed one pebble for every cow leaving a settlement and removed one pebble for every cow returning. The need to count led to the natural numbers, and early mathematicians recorded them with tally marks carved into bone. The Lebombo Bone has 29 uniform notches, while the Ishango Bone has a column grouped as 11, 13, 17, and 19 and another suggesting doubling.
activities.prompt: If another cow leaves the settlement before evening, what should the herder do to keep the record accurate?
options: Add one pebble for the departing cow.
Remove one pebble for the departing cow.
Leave the pebble total unchanged because the cow may return.
Remove two pebbles for the departing cow.

Removing a pebble would reduce the record instead of showing a departure.
why.Leave the pebble total unchanged because: A departure must be recorded even if the cow later returns.
why.Remove two pebbles for the departing cow: One departure corresponds to one added pebble, not two.

activities.explanation: Each departure requires one additional pebble under the stated method.

activities.context: Early people counted because it was a practical need, matching each object with one item. A herder placed one pebble for every cow leaving a settlement and removed one pebble for every cow returning. The need to count led to the natural numbers, and early mathematicians recorded them with tally marks carved into bone. The Lebombo Bone has 29 uniform notches, while the Ishango Bone has a column grouped as 11, 13, 17, and 19 and another suggesting doubling.
activities.prompt: Why does the herder's method make it possible to keep an accurate record of the herd?
options: It matches every departing cow with one added pebble and every returning cow with one removed pebble.
It uses the same single pebble to represent all cows at once.
It changes pebbles into natural numbers without recording individual departures.
It guarantees that no cow can leave or return.

why.It uses the same single pebble to repres: One-to-one matching requires a separate pebble for each cow.
why.It changes pebbles into natural numbers: The method depends on recording each departure and return.
why.It guarantees that no cow can leave or r: Counting tracks movements but does not prevent them.

activities.explanation: The matching action preserves one record item for each cow that is away.

activities.context: A school exhibition asks students to compare ancient trade with number systems. One display represents Lothal, an important urban centre of the Indus Valley Civilisation, and explains why standardised weights and measures were crucial for trade. Another shows the Ṛigveda’s use of quantities expressed in powers of 10. Students then connect India’s place-value system with the development of zero, Brahmagupta’s transformation of the void, and the Bakhśhālī Manuscript’s use of a bold dot called a bindu for zero.
activities.prompt: If the traders at the exhibition could no longer use standardised weights and measures, what would most likely happen?
options: Different traders might judge quantities differently, making exchanges less reliable.
Trade would become more reliable because every trader could set personal rules.
Only calculations involving large numbers would be affected, while ordinary exchanges would remain unchanged.
Trade would remain unchanged because powers of 10 would replace the need for common measurements.

why.Trade would become more reliable because: Personal rules would weaken the common standard needed for trade.
why.Only calculations involving large number: Standardisation affects ordinary exchanges as well as large-number calculations.
why.Trade would remain unchanged because pow: Powers of 10 organise numbers but cannot replace standardised weights and measures.

activities.explanation: Shared measurements help buyers and sellers judge quantities consistently.

activities.context: A school exhibition asks students to compare ancient trade with number systems. One display represents Lothal, an important urban centre of the Indus Valley Civilisation, and explains why standardised weights and measures were crucial for trade. Another shows the Ṛigveda’s use of quantities expressed in powers of 10. Students then connect India’s place-value system with the development of zero, Brahmagupta’s transformation of the void, and the Bakhśhālī Manuscript’s use of a bold dot called a bindu for zero.
activities.prompt: A visitor says that the Bakhśhālī bindu was merely a decorative dot. How should the guide respond?
options: It was a numerical sign: the manuscript’s bindu stood for zero.
It marked the largest quantity, because larger numbers became necessary as civilisations advanced.
It was a general marker for powers of 10 and several other kinds of quantity.
It belonged only to yoga and meditation and was never used as a number.

why.It marked the largest quantity, because: The bindu represented zero rather than the largest quantity.
why.It was a general marker for powers of 10: It was a sign for zero, not a general marker for several kinds of quantity.
why.It belonged only to yoga and meditation: Although Śhūnyatā was a goal of yoga and meditation, the bindu also had a numerical use.

activities.explanation: The Bakhśhālī Manuscript used the bold bindu to represent zero.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): India developed a number system based on place values and powers of 10.
Reason (R): This development helped lead to the idea of zero.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the development of the place-value system directly explains the emergence of the idea of zero.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Brahmagupta transformed the void into a number.
Reason (R): Śhūnyatā was only a goal of yoga and meditation and had no mathematical connection.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the reason is false because Śhūnyatā was connected with Brahmagupta’s mathematical transformation of the void.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between Śhūnyatā as a goal of yoga and meditation and zero as used in number systems?
activities.answer: Śhūnyatā was a goal of yoga and meditation, while its related mathematical development helped produce the idea of zero. India’s number system was based on place values and powers of 10, and this development helped lead to zero. Brahmagupta transformed the void into a number, giving it a mathematical role. The Ṛigveda used quantities expressed in powers of 10, the Babylonians and Mayans used placeholders for empty columns, and the Bakhśhālī Manuscript used a bold bindu for zero. Thus, Śhūnyatā was connected with yoga and meditation, whereas zero became a number represented by symbols.
points: Śhūnyatā was a goal of yoga and meditation.
India’s place-value and powers-of-10 system helped lead to zero.
Brahmagupta transformed the void into a number.
A bindu and placeholders were different ways of representing zero or an empty position.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A trader records a fortune as a positive number and a debt as a negative number. The trader owes a customer a debt and later owes the customer another debt, so the two debts are added. The trader also has a fortune and multiplies it by zero while checking the ledger. Finally, the trader adds zero to the fortune and finds that the fortune remains unchanged.
activities.prompt: If the trader combines the two debts, how should the result be recorded?
options: The combined amount should be recorded as a debt.
The combined amount should be recorded as a fortune.
The combined amount should be recorded as zero.
The combined amount should remain recorded as two separate debts.

why.The combined amount should be recorded a: Adding debts does not produce a fortune.
Adding debts does not produce zero.
why.The combined amount should remain record: The rule gives one combined debt, not two debts.

activities.explanation: A debt plus a debt is a debt.

activities.context: A trader records a fortune as a positive number and a debt as a negative number. The trader owes a customer a debt and later owes the customer another debt, so the two debts are added. The trader also has a fortune and multiplies it by zero while checking the ledger. Finally, the trader adds zero to the fortune and finds that the fortune remains unchanged.
activities.prompt: What happens when the trader adds zero to the fortune?
options: The fortune should stay the same.
The fortune should become zero.
The fortune should become a debt.
The fortune should double.

Adding zero does not make the fortune zero.
Adding zero does not turn a fortune into a debt.
Adding zero does not double a number.

activities.explanation: Adding zero leaves a number unchanged.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Adding zero to a fortune leaves the fortune unchanged.
Reason (R): Adding zero leaves any number unchanged.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason states the rule that directly explains the assertion.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The product of two debts is a fortune.
Reason (R): This happens because the product of a debt and a fortune is a fortune.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the proposed reason is false because a debt multiplied by a fortune gives a debt.

activities.prompt: Explain how zero behaves when it is added to or subtracted from a number.
activities.answer: Zero is the result of subtracting a number from itself. Adding zero to a number leaves that number unchanged, so the trader’s fortune remains a fortune. Subtracting zero from a number also leaves it unchanged, so the fortune does not change in either calculation. Therefore, adding or subtracting zero does not change the value already recorded in the ledger.
points: Defines zero correctly
Explains addition of zero
Explains subtraction of zero
States that the recorded value does not change
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student shares a container of colour with a friend. The whole container is treated as one, so the friend’s portion is represented by a positive rational fraction. Each fraction used is a ratio of integers with a non-zero denominator. An equivalent fraction can represent the same portion. Dividing a common factor from the numerator and denominator produces a lowest form, where the two are co-prime. The opposite portion is represented by the additive inverse of the positive fraction.
activities.prompt: The student has two fraction representations for the friend’s portion. How should the student determine whether they are equal?
options: Compare only the numerators
Compare only the denominators
Cross-multiply and compare the products
Compare only whether the signs match

why.Compare only the numerators: Comparing only numerators leaves out information needed to test equality.
why.Compare only the denominators: Comparing only denominators also leaves out the numerators.
why.Compare only whether the signs match: Matching signs does not show that two rational fractions are equal.

activities.explanation: Cross-multiplication checks whether the products are equal, as required by the equality rule.

activities.context: A student shares a container of colour with a friend. The whole container is treated as one, so the friend’s portion is represented by a positive rational fraction. Each fraction used is a ratio of integers with a non-zero denominator. An equivalent fraction can represent the same portion. Dividing a common factor from the numerator and denominator produces a lowest form, where the two are co-prime. The opposite portion is represented by the additive inverse of the positive fraction.
activities.prompt: If the student changes the positive fraction to represent the opposite share, what should the student do?
options: Keep the positive fraction unchanged
Change only the numerator’s sign
Change the sign of the whole fraction
Replace the denominator with zero

why.Keep the positive fraction unchanged: Keeping the positive sign would not produce the additive inverse.
why.Change only the numerator’s sign: Changing only the numerator’s sign does not necessarily produce the opposite value.
why.Replace the denominator with zero: A zero denominator is not allowed for a rational number.

activities.explanation: Changing the whole fraction’s sign gives the additive inverse of the positive fraction.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A rational number is defined by a ratio of integers whose denominator is non-zero.
Reason (R): The value of a rational number does not depend on choosing one fraction representation rather than another.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the reason explains multiple representations rather than the definition of a rational number.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between a rational number and a fraction representation.
activities.answer: A rational number is defined by a ratio of integers, with a non-zero denominator. A fraction is a way that a rational number may be represented. Because one rational number can have more than one fraction representation, different-looking fractions can still describe the same value. Dividing a common factor from the numerator and denominator gives a lowest-form representation. In lowest form, the numerator and denominator are co-prime.
points: A rational number is a ratio of integers.
The denominator must be non-zero.
One rational number can have several fraction representations.
Lowest form has co-prime numerator and denominator.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): There are infinitely many rational numbers between any two points.
Reason (R): Rational numbers can lie between two integers.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the reason does not explain why infinitely many rational numbers occur between any two points.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The absolute value of a negative number is negative.
Reason (R): The absolute value of a negative number is its positive value.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false, while the reason correctly states the rule.

chapters.title: Exploring Algebraic Identities
chapters.summary: In this chapter: patterns and visualising identities; understanding and using the square identities; factorisation using identities; squares of three terms and difference of squares.

lessons.title: Patterns and Visualising Identities

activities.prompt: Can a square’s shape reveal the secret behind a useful identity?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Seeing an Algebraic Identity
activities.body: An algebraic identity is a rule that is true for every value of its letters. The outer square has area (a + b)². Inside are squares of areas a² and b². Two rectangles each have area ab. These show that (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b². This makes difficult calculations easier. It also works when a and b are negative numbers.
keyPoints: An identity is true for every value of its variables.
The square's pieces give a² + 2ab + b².
The identity works with negative numbers.
activities.explanation: The square's pieces show why the identity is true.

activities.prompt: A child plans a square patio with side a+b. How can its parts reveal a useful identity?
steps: The outer square has side a+b, so its area is (a+b)².
The inner squares have areas a² and b², giving a²+b².
Each rectangle has area ab, so both rectangles add 2ab.
Adding all parts gives the identity and makes difficult calculations easier.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which area belongs to the outer square?
options: (a + b)²
a²
b²
2ab
activities.explanation: The outer square is shown with area (a + b)².

activities.prompt: The two rectangles together have area ______.
activities.hint: Use the area of one rectangle twice.
activities.explanation: Each rectangle has area ab. Together, they have area 2ab.

activities.prompt: Which statement must describe an algebraic identity?
options: An identity need not be true for all values of its variables.
An identity is true for every value of its variables.
An identity changes when its variables change.
An identity can fail for some values of its variables.
activities.explanation: An algebraic identity is true for every value of its variables.

activities.prompt: Match each part of the square picture to its area.
activities.explanation: Each pair matches the area assigned to that part of the square picture.

activities.prompt: Which statement about values of a and b is correct?
options: It works with negative values and also with line-segment lengths.
It works only with values used as line-segment lengths.
It fails with negative values but works with line-segment lengths.
It works with negative values but fails with line-segment lengths.
activities.explanation: The identity works with negative values. It also holds for line-segment lengths.

activities.prompt: Match each statement to its correct description.
pairs: True for every value of its variables
Need not be true for all values
The identity holds for all such values
activities.explanation: Identities hold for every value. Ordinary equations need not. Negative values work, and line-segment lengths also work.

activities.prompt: A square playground has side a+b. It contains squares a² and b², plus two rectangles. Which expression gives the whole area?
options: a² + 2ab + b²
a² + ab + b²
a² + 2a² + b²
2a² + 2ab + b²

why.a² + ab + b²: This counts only one rectangle, leaving another ab missing.
why.a² + 2a² + b²: This doubles a² instead of using the smaller square area b².
why.2a² + 2ab + b²: This doubles a² and changes the total area.

activities.explanation: This adds both square areas and both rectangle areas.

activities.prompt: A student wants to verify (a + b)² using the distributive property. Which step should the student take?
options: Write (a + b)(a + b), then distribute each part.
Draw the inner squares and ignore the rectangles.
Use only a² and b², then stop there.
Set a and b to one positive length.

why.Draw the inner squares and ignore the re: Drawing only squares leaves out the two rectangle areas.
Stopping at a² and b² leaves out both rectangle areas.
One length checks only a special case, not every value.

activities.explanation: This uses the distributive property to expand the square.

activities.prompt: A tiled floor shows inner squares a² and b². Its two rectangles each have area ab. What is missing from the sum a²+b²?
options: The missing area is 2ab, from both rectangles.
The missing area is ab, from one rectangle.
The missing area is a²+b², from both squares.
The missing area is 2(a+b)², from the whole square.

why.The missing area is ab, from one rectang: Only one rectangle is counted, leaving another ab missing.
why.The missing area is a²+b², from both squ: These are already the inner square areas, not the missing area.
why.The missing area is 2(a+b)², from the wh: This is twice the whole square, not the missing rectangle area.

activities.explanation: Both rectangles add 2ab, so this completes the square’s area.

lessons.title: Understanding and Using the Square Identities

activities.prompt: Ready to discover the secret pattern inside a squared sum?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Square-of-a-Sum Identity
activities.body: Squares of sums have a useful pattern. You can expand (x + y)² as x² + 2xy + y². This pattern works for all x and y. In general, (a + b)² is not equal to a² + b². The expansion helps you compare expressions. It also helps you calculate squares, such as writing 43² as (40 + 3)². Remember the middle term, 2xy.
keyPoints: Expanding (x + y)² gives x² + 2xy + y².
The expansion can compare expressions.
Write 43² as (40 + 3)².
activities.explanation: The middle term makes the square of a sum complete.

activities.prompt: A student has 10 large cards and 2 small cards. Should squaring the total equal adding the two square groups?
steps: The two groups have sizes a and b, so their total is a + b.
Squaring the total gives (a + b)², so we compare it with a² + b².
Here a = 10 and b = 2, and the sum of the squares is 104.
The square of the sum is greater in this example, so the two methods are different.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: The identity (x + y)² = x² + 2xy + y² works for all x and y.
activities.explanation: Exactly! This identity works for every x and y.

activities.prompt: When you expand (x + y)², the middle term is ______.
activities.hint: Use the square-of-a-sum identity.
activities.explanation: The identity is x² + 2xy + y², so the middle term is 2xy.

activities.prompt: Which expression equals (x + y)²?
options: x² + y²
x² + 2xy + y²
2x² + 2xy + y²
x² + 2xy + 2y²
activities.explanation: The square-of-a-sum identity includes the middle term 2xy.

activities.prompt: Match each square with its correct expansion or value.
activities.explanation: Each pair follows the square-of-a-sum identity or the given square calculation.

activities.prompt: Put the steps for calculating 43² in order.
activities.explanation: The expansion follows the square-of-a-sum identity and gives 43² = 1849.

activities.prompt: For a = 10 and b = 2, which expression is greater?
options: a² + b²
(a + b)²
a²
b²
activities.explanation: Here, a² + b² = 104, and (a + b)² is greater.

activities.prompt: When expanding (5x + 2y)², which expression is correct?
options: 25x² + 20xy + 4y²
25x² + 10xy + 4y²
5x² + 20xy + 2y²
25x² + 20xy + 2y²
activities.explanation: Use 5x as the first term and 2y as the second term. The identity gives 25x² + 20xy + 4y².

activities.prompt: Which claim about x² – 1 = 24 is correct?
options: It holds only for x = 5.
It holds only for x = –5.
It holds for x = 5 and x = –5.

activities.prompt: Can you uncover secret shortcuts that make tricky rational expressions much simpler?

activities.title: Finding and Cancelling Common Factors
activities.body: Factorisation can help us simplify rational algebraic expressions. We simplify a rational expression by cancelling common numerator and denominator factors. For example, x² – 7x + 12 is shown as two multiplied brackets, (x – 3)(x – 4). Another denominator, 5x² + 5x – 100, has a common factor of 5. It becomes 5(x – 4)(x + 5).
keyPoints: Factorisation helps simplify rational expressions.
Cancel common numerator and denominator factors.
Factoring helps us find common factors.
activities.explanation: Factorisation reveals common factors, which can then be cancelled when they are not zero.

activities.prompt: A classroom has (6 - 4)(6 - 3) chairs arranged in (6 - 4) equal rows. How many chairs are in each row?
steps: There are 6 chairs and 2 rows.
Cancel the common factor 2 from the total and the number of rows.
Each row has 3 chairs.

Factor the denominator as 5(x – 4)(x + 5) because five is common.
Cancel x – 4 because it is common and not zero.
The simplified expression is (x – 3)/(5(x + 5)), because the other factors remain.

keyPoints: Both parts must share the same factor.
The common factor here is x – 4.
The common factor is not equal to zero.

activities.context: During a school mathematics activity, a student is checking a square design. The outer square is divided into a larger square with area a², a smaller square with area b², and two rectangles, each with area ab. The student wants to confirm the total area and decide how to check the result for every value of a and b.
activities.prompt: Which equation should the student use for the total area of the outer square?
options: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²
(a + b)² = a² + ab + b²
(a + b)² = 2a² + 2b²
(a + b)² = a² + 2ab

why.(a + b)² = a² + ab + b²: It counts only one of the two rectangles.
why.(a + b)² = 2a² + 2b²: It treats each inner-square area as appearing twice.
why.(a + b)² = a² + 2ab: It leaves out the area of the smaller inner square.

activities.explanation: It adds the areas of both rectangles and both inner squares.

activities.context: During a school mathematics activity, a student is checking a square design. The outer square is divided into a larger square with area a², a smaller square with area b², and two rectangles, each with area ab. The student wants to confirm the total area and decide how to check the result for every value of a and b.
activities.prompt: What should the student do to verify the identity for every value of a and b?
options: Use the distributive property and compare the expansion with the sum of the areas.
Check the consecutive-square pattern and rely on that pattern alone.
Test one positive value and treat the result as proof for every value.
Rearrange an ordinary equation until it is true for one chosen value.

why.Check the consecutive-square pattern and: A pattern that seems to work does not prove the identity generally.
why.Test one positive value and treat the re: One tested value does not establish the identity for every value.
why.Rearrange an ordinary equation until it: An ordinary equation need not be true for all values.

activities.explanation: The distributive property verifies the equality for every value.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The algebraic identity can be verified using the distributive property.
Reason (R): The distributive property gives a² + 2ab + b², which matches the sum of the areas of the four parts.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The stated expansion accounts for all four areas and therefore verifies the identity.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The identity (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² also works when a and b are negative numbers.
Reason (R): The identity can be used only when a and b are line-segment lengths.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason is false because the identity also works for negative values.

activities.prompt: Explain how the areas of the four parts of the design lead to the algebraic identity.
activities.answer: The outer square has area (a + b)². Inside it, the larger square contributes a² and the smaller square contributes b². The two rectangles each contribute ab, so together they contribute 2ab. Adding all four areas gives (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b². Using the distributive property gives the same result: (a + b)(a + b) = a² + ab + ab + b². Therefore, the diagram and algebra verify the identity for every value of a and b, including negative values.
points: Identifies the outer-square area.
Uses a² and b² for the inner squares.
Adds the two rectangle areas as 2ab.
Uses the distributive property to verify the identity.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

activities.prompt: How does the square-of-a-sum identity help us calculate 43²?
activities.answer: To calculate 43², begin by writing 43 as 40 + 3 and use (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b². This turns the square of the whole number into the squares of 40 and 3 plus their cross term. Completing the calculation gives 43² = 1849. The method is useful because it shows how the square-of-a-sum identity expands a general binomial expression instead of treating the original number as an unexplained result.
points: Writes 43 as 40 + 3.
Uses the square-of-a-sum identity.
Includes the extra product term in the expansion.
Gives the calculation 43² = 1849.

activities.context: At a school revision table, a student is checking two algebra examples. For the first, the student notices that x² + 4x + 4 has the square-of-a-sum pattern. For the second, the student sees that 36x² + 12x + 1 can be rewritten in the same pattern and that 2 is common to all three terms. The student wants to finish both factorisations and explain which identity appears when a negative value replaces b.
activities.prompt: Which expression is a factor of the first polynomial?

why.x + 4: x + 4 wrongly uses 4 instead of 2 as the added number.

activities.context: At a school revision table, a student is checking two algebra examples. For the first, the student notices that x² + 4x + 4 has the square-of-a-sum pattern. For the second, the student sees that 36x² + 12x + 1 can be rewritten in the same pattern and that 2 is common to all three terms. The student wants to finish both factorisations and explain which identity appears when a negative value replaces b.
activities.prompt: Which identity results when b is replaced by negative b?
options: (a - b)² = a² - 2ab + b²
(a + b)² = a² - 2ab + b²

(a + b)² = a² - 2ab - b²

why.(a + b)² = a² - 2ab + b²: The second option keeps the plus sign in the middle despite changing b to negative b.
why.(a - b)² = a² + 2ab + b²: The third option changes b but wrongly keeps the plus sign in the middle.
why.(a + b)² = a² - 2ab - b²: The fourth option changes the sign of the final term as well as the middle term.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): x² + 4x + 4 = (x + 2)².
Reason (R): The expression matches a² + 2ab + b² with a = x and b = 2.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

activities.prompt:

Reason (R): Replacing b by negative b gives another useful identity.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

activities.prompt: Explain how the square-of-a-sum identity can be used to factor 36x² + 12x + 1.
activities.answer: The expression 36x² + 12x + 1 can be written as a² + 2ab + b² by choosing a = 6x and b = 1, because (6x)² = 36x², 2(6x)(1) = 12x, and 1² = 1. Applying the square-of-a-sum identity then gives (6x + 1)². This shows how recognising the pattern turns the expression into one squared factor.

chapters.summary: In this chapter: circles and their parts; symmetry and circles through points; chords and angles at the centre; midpoints and distances of chords.

lessons.title: Circles and Their Parts

activities.prompt: What makes a circle so special, and what are its parts called?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet the Parts of a Circle
activities.body: A circle consists of all points in a plane equally distant from one fixed point. That fixed point is its centre. A locus is the set of points meeting a given condition. The radius is the distance from the centre to any point on the circle. A chord has both ends on the circle. A diameter is a chord passing through the centre.
keyPoints: Every circle point is equally distant from the centre.
The radius runs from the centre to the circle.
A diameter is a chord passing through the centre.
activities.explanation: These words name the main parts and definitions of a circle.

activities.prompt: A circle has centre C. Point P lies on the circle, and CP is 8 cm. What is the radius of the circle, in cm?
steps: The given centre-to-point distance is 8 cm.
A centre-to-point distance is a radius, so the radius is 8 cm.

activities.explanation: The fixed point in the definition of a circle is called its centre.

activities.prompt: A and B lie on a circular wheel, the straight segment AB passes through its centre O, and the radius is 3 cm. What is the length of AB, in cm?
activities.explanation: A chord that passes through the centre is a diameter. The diameter is two radii, so 6 = 2 x 3 cm. Therefore, AB is 6 cm.
steps: A chord that passes through the centre is a diameter.
The diameter is two radii, so 6 = 2 x 3 cm.
Therefore, AB is 6 cm.
activities.hint: Use the two equal radii that make a diameter.

It is only a chord, because passing through the centre changes nothing.
It is a locus, because its two ends meet one condition.

why.It is a radius, because it joins the cen: This mistake treats a centre-to-edge segment as a full crossing segment.
why.It is only a chord, because passing thro: This mistake forgets that a chord through the centre is a diameter.
why.It is a locus, because its two ends meet: This mistake confuses a segment with a set of points meeting one condition.

activities.explanation: This is right because a diameter is a chord through the centre.

why.A diameter must have one end exactly at: This mistake thinks a diameter is a centre-to-edge segment.
why.A chord cannot have both ends lying on t: This mistake denies that a chord can join two circle points.

why.The first segment is a chord; the second: This mistake treats the first segment as having two circle ends.
why.The first segment is a radius; the secon: This mistake ignores that the second segment passes through the centre.

activities.explanation: Right: the first joins centre to edge; the second crosses the centre.

lessons.title: Symmetry and Circles Through Points

activities.prompt: Where might the centre be for a circle passing through two points?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Circle Symmetry and Centres
activities.body: A circle looks unchanged after any rotation. This is rotational symmetry. Reflection symmetry means both halves match when folded. A folding crease on circular paper is such a line. Every diameter is also such a line. Points A and B can lie on infinitely many circles. Their centres are equally distant from A and B. These centres lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB. This line passes through the midpoint at right angles.
keyPoints: A circle has rotational symmetry.
A crease and every diameter are reflection-symmetry lines.
Centres of circles through A and B lie on one perpendicular bisector.
activities.explanation: Symmetry describes how a circle can turn or fold without changing.

activities.prompt: Points A and B are 10 cm apart, and a circle centred at the midpoint of AB passes through both points. What is the radius of the circle in cm?
steps: The centre is the midpoint of the 10 cm segment AB.
The midpoint is half the distance from A to B.
10 divided by 2 = 5 cm, so the answer is 5 cm.

{d} divided by 2 = {radius} cm, so the answer is {answer} cm.

activities.prompt: You have two marked points and want to draw a circle through both.
steps: Midpoint AB is equally distant from A and B.
It therefore works as a centre for a circle through both.
Other equal-distance points work, because their circles also reach both.
So infinitely many circles can pass through A and B.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: One Circle Through a Triangle
activities.body: Three non-collinear points are points that do not lie on one straight line. Exactly one circle passes through them. Its centre is the circumcentre of the triangle. The circumcentre lies inside an acute-angled triangle, one with sharp angles. It lies outside an obtuse-angled triangle, one with a wide angle. For a right-angled triangle, it is the midpoint of the hypotenuse. The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle.
keyPoints: Three non-collinear points lie on exactly one circle.
The centre of that circle is the circumcentre.
The circumcentre's position depends on the triangle's angle type.
activities.explanation: These rules help you find and locate the centre of a triangle's circle.

lessons.title: Chords and Angles at the Centre

activities.prompt: Why do equal chords make equal angles at the centre?

activities.title: Equal Chords and Central Angles
activities.body: A tight thread fixed at two points can be thought of as a chord. Turning a wheel makes the thread another chord of equal length. “Subtend” means “make an angle at”. Equal chords make equal central angles. Radii joining chord ends are equal. These equal sides prove both triangles congruent by SSS. A chord and centre form an isosceles triangle with two equal sides.
keyPoints: Equal chords make equal central angles.
Equal radii and chords prove congruence by SSS.
A chord and centre form an isosceles triangle.
activities.explanation: Equal chords and equal radii help prove equal central angles.

activities.prompt: Chord A subtends an angle of 70 degrees at the centre of a circle. Chord B has the same length as chord A. What central angle does chord B subtend?
steps: Chord A subtends 70 degrees at the centre.
Equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre, so chord B has the same central angle.
Therefore, chord B subtends 70 degrees.

This is why the whole circle is defined as all points in a plane that are equally distant from one fixed point. The equal-distance condition is what makes the shape a circle, while the centre and radius identify its fixed point and equal distance.

activities.title: Perimeter and the C/D ratio
activities.body: Perimeter is the distance around a shape’s border. A square with side a has perimeter 4a units. An equilateral triangle has perimeter 3a units. A rectangle has perimeter 2(a + b) units. The square formula is a special rectangle case. A circle’s perimeter is usually called circumference. The C/D ratio compares circumference with diameter. It stays unchanged as size changes. Mesopotamians went beyond 3 for pi. Archimedes trapped pi between polygon perimeters.
keyPoints: Perimeter measures distance around a border.
C/D ratio stays unchanged as size changes.
Circle perimeter is usually called circumference.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect shape formulas with the constant C/D ratio.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: The story and nature of pi

activities.prompt: How did people across centuries uncover the secrets of pi?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How people understood pi
activities.body: Zu Chongzhi used polygons with 24,576 sides to estimate pi. He discovered Yuelü, meaning “Approximate Ratio.” Āryabhaṭa gave 20000, equal to 3.1416, and called it asanna, meaning approaching or approximate. Mādhava saw pi as a limit, not just a number to approximate, and used a sum without an end. Pi is irrational, so no ratio of two integers equals it. Its digits do not show the repeating pattern found in fractions.
keyPoints: Zu Chongzhi estimated pi and discovered Yuelü.
Āryabhaṭa gave 20000 and called his value asanna.
Mādhava treated pi as a limit and used an infinite series.
activities.explanation: These ideas show how people moved from close estimates to deeper understanding.

activities.title: Unroll the circle

activities.takeaway: Every circle goes round about 3.14 diameters, which is π. Circumference = 2πr and area = πr².

steps: Zu Chongzhi's estimate used 24,576 sides, but estimates cannot equal irrational pi.

Lambert's proof means pi cannot equal any ratio of two integers.
Therefore, no fraction is exactly pi, and no best fraction can exist.

activities.title: Arcs and the 400 m track
activities.body: An arc is a circle’s curved part. A semicircle has arc length πr. A quarter circle has arc length πr divided by 2. The 400 m track has two straight sections of 84.39 m each. Its curved portions are semicircles with a common centre. Each lane is 1.22 m wide. The athlete’s two semicircles have radius 36.8 m and form one complete circle. Staggers help make running distances fair.
keyPoints: A semicircle has arc length πr.

activities.title: Circle paths and area facts
activities.body: The equal-radius circles are congruent because their radii match. Their centres and an intersection form an equilateral triangle, with all sides equal. The two half-circle paths between P and Q have equal length. Area means space occupied by a flat, two-dimensional region, measured in square units. A parallelogram can become a rectangle with the same area. A triangle’s area is half its base × height. A line called a median makes two equal-area triangles.
keyPoints: The equal-radius circles are congruent.
The two half-circle paths between P and Q have equal length.
A triangle’s area is half its base × height.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect equal-length paths with area facts.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Triangle and 4-gon area formulas

activities.title: Heron’s and Brahmagupta’s formulas
activities.body: Heron’s formula gives a triangle’s area from its three side lengths. It multiplies four terms involving the semi-perimeter and sides. A triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 has a semi-perimeter of 6 units. Brahmagupta’s formula generalises Heron’s formula. It needs the special property of a cyclic 4-gon, a four-sided shape. Side lengths alone do not determine a 4-gon’s area.
keyPoints: Heron’s formula uses the three side lengths.
It multiplies four terms involving the semi-perimeter and sides.
A triangle can be a cyclic 4-gon with one zero-length side.
activities.explanation: These facts connect Heron’s formula with Brahmagupta’s formula for cyclic 4-gons.

activities.prompt: A four-sided garden has measured sides. Nobody checked whether it is cyclic. Can Brahmagupta’s formula be used yet?

Heron’s formula instead uses a triangle’s three side lengths.
A triangle is a special cyclic 4-gon with one zero-length side.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Squaring a rectangle and area of a circle

activities.prompt: Can we turn a rectangle into a square without changing its area?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Equal areas and circle areas
activities.body: Squaring a rectangle means constructing a square with the same area. Baudhāyana showed this in his 800 BCE Śhulbasūtra. His square HPQS matches the area of rectangle ABCD. Circular shapes have long been used in settlements, buildings and tools. For a circle, area is πr², where r is the radius. A sector is bounded by an arc and two radii. Its area uses the central angle and 360°.
keyPoints: Squaring gives an equal-area square.
The area of a circle is πr².
A sector's area uses πr², its central angle and 360°.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect equal areas with the special formula for circles.

activities.prompt: A designer needs a square design with the same area as rectangle ABCD. How can Baudhāyana’s construction help?

Choose square HPQS, because the construction gives it the same area.
Keep that area unchanged, because equal area is the goal of squaring.

Around 1500 BCE: Egyptians produced a more accurate circle-area formula
About 250 BCE: Archimedes showed that the constant is pi
activities.explanation: Baudhāyana's work came first, followed by the Egyptian formula and then Archimedes.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between the approaches of Āryabhaṭa, Zu Chongzhi, and Mādhava toward pi.
activities.answer: Āryabhaṭa’s 20000 was called asanna because it approached pi rather than giving it exactly. Zu Chongzhi’s Yuelü, the Approximate Ratio, also reflects the use of an estimate: he used a polygon with 24,576 sides. Mādhava’s idea was different. He regarded pi as a limit and gave an exact formula involving an infinite series. Thus, an approximation is a value used to approach pi, while the limit idea and exact formula describe pi through an infinite series, not as a ratio of two integers.
points: The value 20000 was named asanna and treated as approximate.
Zu Chongzhi used a 24,576-sided polygon and called his estimate the Yuelü.
Mādhava regarded pi as a limit.
His exact formula used an infinite series rather than a ratio of two integers.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A school athlete trains on a 400 m track. Its two straight sections are each 84.39 m long, giving 168.78 m in total. activities.title: Understanding probability
activities.body: Probability is a measurement for judging how likely an event is. It helps describe confidence or certainty. A random event has an element of chance. Its result cannot be known in advance. Some judgements use a person's interpretation of evidence. This is called subjective probability. Objective estimates use collected evidence. Learning both helps you estimate uncertainty fairly.
keyPoints: Probability judges how likely events are.
Random events contain an element of chance.
Objective estimates use collected evidence.

activities.title: Understanding randomness
activities.body: Randomness means you cannot predict exactly what will happen. You may know all possible outcomes without knowing which one will definitely occur. Probability is the part of mathematics that studies randomness. It is measured on a scale from 0 to 1. A probability of 0 means that an event is impossible. A probability of 1 means that an event is certain to happen.

activities.title: Two ways to estimate probability
activities.body: Probability can be estimated in two main ways: through experience or theory. Experience comes from repeated experiments or past observations. Experimental probability uses relative frequency. This means how often the wanted result happened in actual trials. Theoretical probability assumes that all possible outcomes are equally likely. An experiment's result is an outcome. The sample space lists all possible outcomes.
keyPoints: Experimental probability uses relative frequency.
Theoretical probability assumes equal chances.
The sample space lists every possible outcome.
activities.explanation: Experiments use actual results, while theory uses equal chances.

activities.title: Two ways to study chance
activities.body: Theoretical probability studies how likely an event is when outcomes are equally likely. An event is an outcome being studied. It describes what should happen in a perfectly fair situation. You need no experiment or data to use it. Favourable outcomes match the event. Probability divides favourable outcomes by possible outcomes. Usually, it uses P for an event or outcome. Statistical data means information used for work in business and research.
keyPoints: Theoretical probability describes a perfectly fair situation.
It divides favourable outcomes by possible outcomes.
Statistical data is used for practical work in business and research.
activities.explanation: Each idea connects fair outcomes with information used in practical work.

activities.title: Sample spaces and events
activities.body: A sample space lists every possible outcome of a situation. Each outcome is one element. No outcome is listed twice. The number of elements is the sample size. An event is one result or a group of results. Every event is a subset of its sample space. For example, rain has two outcomes: Rain and No Rain.

An event is one result or a group of results.

activities.prompt: Why is it important to learn how to estimate probability objectively?
activities.answer: Probability is a type of measurement used to judge how likely events are and to describe how confident or certain we are. A random event contains chance because its result cannot be known in advance, so probability describes uncertainty rather than guaranteeing an outcome. A judgement can depend on different kinds of evidence. Objective estimates use collected evidence rather than only personal opinions. Learning this method helps the class avoid presenting a personal interpretation as a certain or objective conclusion.

activities.prompt: Explain why knowing all possible outcomes does not make a random result predictable.
activities.answer: Knowing all possible outcomes tells us only what can happen, not which result will definitely occur. When a die is rolled, its possible results are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6, but a particular result cannot be predicted exactly. The roll can be repeated, and the result might be different each time. Similarly, in a lucky draw, every student has an equal chance of being selected, so knowing who is eligible does not reveal who will be chosen.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between experimental probability and theoretical probability.
activities.answer: Experimental probability is estimated from actual observations. It is found by using the relative frequency of an event, so it depends on what happened during repeated experiments. In the die experiment, the student used fifty trials and the number of four outcomes to estimate the chance of rolling a four. Theoretical probability is different: it assumes that all possible outcomes are equally likely. Therefore, experimental probability uses collected data, while theoretical probability uses an equal-likelihood assumption rather than observed results.

Relative frequency is used to estimate experimental probability.
The die estimate uses fifty trials.
Theoretical probability assumes equal likelihood.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Sequences and Patterns

activities.prompt: What if the numbers around you were hiding a pattern?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Sequences
activities.body: Patterns help us make sense of the world and predict what comes next. A sequence is a special pattern made from numbers or other objects. Its items follow a particular order. Each number in a sequence is called a term. Three dots show that the sequence continues indefinitely. The sequence 6, 12, 24, 48, 96 is finite and has five terms.
keyPoints: Sequences are ordered patterns of numbers or objects.
Each number in a sequence is a term.
Three dots show that a sequence continues indefinitely.
activities.explanation: Sequences have ordered terms, and some continue indefinitely.

activities.title: Rules in Number Sequences
activities.body: Some number sequences continue indefinitely. These are called infinite sequences. Natural, odd, triangular and square numbers are all infinite. Natural numbers increase by one each step. Odd numbers increase by two each step. Consecutive terms follow one another. A difference is the gap between terms next to each other. Triangular differences begin 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Square differences begin 3, 5, 7, 9, 11.
keyPoints: Natural numbers increase by one each step.
Odd numbers increase by two each step.
Each number sequence has its own pattern of differences.
activities.explanation: Learning each rule helps you predict the next term.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Explicit Rules for Sequences

activities.prompt: Can you find a sequence’s next term without calculating every term before it?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Using an Explicit Rule
activities.body: A term is a number in a sequence. An explicit formula uses a position number, written as n, to calculate a term’s value. Substituting means replacing n with a chosen value. Different values give the sequence’s terms. The rule un = 2n – 1 generates odd numbers. It can find any term without earlier terms. It can also check whether a number belongs and find a term’s position.
keyPoints: An explicit formula uses the position number n.
Replacing n gives the terms of a sequence.
An explicit rule can find terms, check numbers and find positions.
activities.explanation: Replacing n lets you calculate and check sequence terms.

activities.prompt: The odd-number sequence has the rule u_n = 2n – 1. The number 21 belongs to this sequence. What is its position?
steps: To find the position, set 2n – 1 equal to 21.
Add 1 to both sides and divide by 2 to find n.
(21 + 1) divided by 2 = 11, so the position is 11.

({x} + 1) divided by 2 = {answer}, so the position is {answer}.
gen.hint: Set the rule equal to the given number and solve for n.

activities.title: What is a recursive rule?
activities.body: A recursive rule tells you how to find a term by using earlier terms. You need those terms before you can use the rule. For example, the sequence is 1, 4, 7, 10, 13. Each term is 3 more than the one before it. Later terms can also help you check whether 133 belongs to a sequence.

Later terms can help check whether 133 belongs.

activities.title: Understanding arithmetic progressions
activities.body: An arithmetic progression is a special sequence with the same difference between consecutive terms. This fixed difference is called the common difference. For example, 1, 4, 7, 10, … has common difference 3. The first term is a, and d is the common difference. The nth term means the term at position n. Its rule is tn = a + (n – 1) × d.
keyPoints: Counting tiny squares at each stage produces a sequence.
At each stage, 4 squares are added to the corners.
The square pattern has nth term 4n – 3.
activities.explanation: You have learned the main ideas of arithmetic progressions.

activities.title: Spot the repeating gap

tasks.say: Look at the first two terms.
tasks.then: The next term is always 2 more than the term before.

tasks.say: Move through several more terms and compare each pair.
tasks.then: The gap stays the same, so the terms form an arithmetic progression.

tasks.say: Try a later term.
tasks.then: The fixed difference between consecutive terms is still 2.

activities.takeaway: An arithmetic progression has the same difference between every pair of consecutive terms.
activities.explanation: An arithmetic progression has the same difference between every pair of consecutive terms.

activities.prompt: A child makes a square pattern. Each stage adds 4 corner squares. How can we find the count at any stage?
steps: Because each stage adds 4 squares, d = 4.
The first term is 1, so a = 1.
Therefore, tn = 1 + (n – 1) × 4.
This simplifies to tn = 4n – 3 for any stage.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: One difference or different differences?

activities.title: Pairing to Find a Sum
activities.body: Let Sn mean the sum of the first n natural numbers. First, write this sum in order. Then write it again in reverse order. A pair means two numbers placed together. For the first ten natural numbers, each pair adds to 11. Add the two written forms. This gives twice S, or 2S, equal to n(n + 1). Thus, 2S is 110 and S is 55 for the first ten numbers.
keyPoints: Reversing and adding gives twice S.
2S equals n(n + 1).
For the first ten numbers, S equals 55.
activities.explanation: Pairing makes the reversed sum reveal twice the total.

Adding the ends skips the average of the first and last terms.
Subtracting the ends finds a difference, not the average.

Subtracting S₂₅ removes one term too many from the range.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Geometric Progressions and Fractals

activities.prompt: How can numbers and shapes grow in surprising ways?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Geometric Progressions and Fractals
activities.body: A geometric progression is a sequence in which each term comes from multiplying the previous term by the same number. This number is called the common ratio. In the green-square pattern, each term doubles. A fractal is a shape or pattern that repeats itself at different scales.
keyPoints: A geometric progression multiplies each term by a constant.
The common ratio is the constant multiplier.
Fractals repeat at different scales.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect changing patterns with repeating shapes.

activities.title: Spot the doubling pattern

tasks.say: Move to term 1 and look at the first group.
tasks.then: The sequence begins with 1.

tasks.say: Move to term 4 and compare the last two groups.
tasks.then: Each new term is twice the previous term.

tasks.say: Move to term 8 and compare neighbouring groups.
tasks.then: The multiplier stays 2, so the common ratio is 2.

activities.takeaway: A geometric progression can grow by multiplying every term by the same constant ratio.
activities.explanation: A geometric progression can grow by multiplying every term by the same constant ratio.

activities.prompt: A child notices that a green-square display changes from 3 to 6, then 12, then 24. Why is this a geometric progression?
steps: The green-square pattern gives these four terms in order.
Doubling each previous term gives the next term.
A sequence with the same multiplier at every step is a geometric progression.
The common ratio is the name for that unchanged multiplier.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Each term in the green-square pattern is twice the previous term.
activities.explanation: Each stage doubles the number of green squares.

activities.prompt: The constant multiplier in the green-square pattern is ______.
activities.hint: Look for the number that doubles each term.
activities.explanation: The multiplier is 2, so every term is obtained by doubling.

activities.prompt: Which expression gives the nth term of a GP?
options: a + r
a − r
a × rⁿ⁻¹
rⁿ − a
activities.explanation: The nth term of a GP is written as a × rⁿ⁻¹.

activities.prompt: Which phrase matches the lesson’s definition of a fractal?
options: Repeats at different scales
Changes by adding one
Uses only green squares
Has a common ratio
activities.explanation: A fractal repeats itself at different scales.

activities.prompt: A geometric progression has first term 2 and common ratio 3. What number is its second term?
activities.explanation: The first term is 2. To find the second term, multiply the first term by the common ratio 3. 2 x 3 = 6.
steps: The first term is 2.
To find the second term, multiply the first term by the common ratio 3.
activities.hint: Multiply the first term by the common ratio.

gen.template: A geometric progression has first term {a} and common ratio {r}. What number is its second term?
steps: The first term is {a}.
To find the second term, multiply the first term by the common ratio {r}.
{a} x {r} = {answer}.
gen.hint: Multiply the first term by the common ratio.

wrongWhy.a*r*r: You multiplied twice and found the third term.

activities.prompt: A bus company has 3 buses in the first year. The number of buses is multiplied by 3 each year. How many buses does it have in year 3?
activities.explanation: The first-year count is 3 buses and the yearly multiplier is 3. The nth term uses the first term multiplied by the common ratio 3 minus 1 times. 3 x 3^(3 - 1) = 27 buses.
steps: The first-year count is 3 buses and the yearly multiplier is 3.
The nth term uses the first term multiplied by the common ratio 3 minus 1 times.
activities.hint: Use the first-year count and multiply by the yearly multiplier once for each later year.

gen.template: A bus company has {a} buses in the first year. The number of buses is multiplied by {r} each year. How many buses does it have in year {n}?
steps: The first-year count is {a} buses and the yearly multiplier is {r}.
The nth term uses the first term multiplied by the common ratio {n} minus 1 times.
{a} x {r}^({n} - 1) = {answer} buses.
gen.hint: Use the first-year count and multiply by the yearly multiplier once for each later year.

activities.prompt: A sticker sheet starts with 3 stickers. Each round doubles the total. Which list shows the first four rounds?

why.3, 6, 9, 12: This list adds 3 each time instead of doubling.
why.6, 12, 24, 3: This list starts at 6 instead of the first term 3.
why.12, 24, 3, 6: This list puts the later terms before the first term.

activities.explanation: Doubling 3 gives 6, then 12, then 24.

activities.prompt: A toy pattern starts with 6 shapes. Every stage doubles the count. Which formula gives its nth term?
options: tₙ = 6 × 2ⁿ⁻¹
tₙ = 6 × 2ⁿ
tₙ = 2 × 6ⁿ⁻¹
tₙ = 2ⁿ⁻¹ × 6

why.tₙ = 6 × 2ⁿ: This uses one extra factor of 2 in the exponent.
why.tₙ = 2 × 6ⁿ⁻¹: This swaps the first term with the common ratio.
why.tₙ = 2ⁿ⁻¹ × 6: This reverses the roles of the first term and ratio.

activities.explanation: The first term is 6, and the common ratio is 2.

activities.prompt: A paper pattern starts with 3. Every later term doubles the previous term. Which recursive rule matches it?
options: tₙ = 2tₙ₋₁ for n ≥ 2
tₙ = 3tₙ₋₁ for n ≥ 2
tₙ = tₙ₋₁ + 2 for n ≥ 2
tₙ = 2tₙ for n ≥ 1

why.tₙ = 3tₙ₋₁ for n ≥ 2: This multiplies by 3 instead of the common ratio 2.
why.tₙ = tₙ₋₁ + 2 for n ≥ 2: This adds 2 instead of multiplying the previous term.
why.tₙ = 2tₙ for n ≥ 1: This uses the current term, so it cannot find a new term.

activities.explanation: This doubles the previous term, beginning with the second term.

activities.prompt: Rows contain 3, 6, 12, and 24 cards. A child claims the common ratio is 24. Why is this wrong?
options: The multiplier between every pair of terms is 2.
The largest term in the sequence is the common ratio.
The number of terms shown is the common ratio.
The first term times two is the common ratio.
activities.explanation: Think about why, using the idea from the lesson.

activities.prompt: Each of 9 black triangles is replaced by three smaller triangles. How many black triangles appear next?
options: 1 black triangle
3 black triangles
27 black triangles
9 black triangles

why.1 black triangle: This counts one triangle instead of replacing all nine.
why.3 black triangles: This keeps an earlier stage instead of finding the next stage.
why.9 black triangles: This keeps the current count instead of replacing every triangle.

activities.explanation: Each of 9 triangles makes 3, giving 27 triangles.
